Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette:
Amara is an 80-year-old pastor from a West African country that collapsed into civil war nearly a decade ago. She and her husband fled after armed men stormed her church during Sunday service, swinging machetes and firing into the pews. Amara had been at the altar; she saw two deacons killed and heard a young mother scream before being cut down. She escaped through a back door and ran for days, eventually crossing the border. Now she lives in a small American city, still serving a tiny congregation of fellow refugees. But the memory of that morning invades her mind without warning: the crack of gunfire, the wet sound of blades, the screams—she hears them in her head as if they are happening again, so vivid that she sometimes has to touch her own arm to convince herself it is real. The memory feels so extreme, so beyond anything she ever imagined, that she often wonders if it truly happened to her or if she dreamed it.

These intrusions are most likely to come while she is riding the bus. Amara relies on public transport to reach her church, but the crowded space, the sudden stops, and the press of strangers trigger a sense of unreality—a feeling that she is beginning to float away, detached from her own body. As soon as that dissociative feeling starts, she pulls a heavy scarf up around her face and hunches into a shapeless coat, hoping to become invisible. She cannot bear to be seen; she is certain that if someone notices her, they will know she is a target. She also finds herself watching every passenger, especially men, for any sudden movement. A man reaching into his pocket makes her chest tighten; she immediately looks behind her to see if someone is following. In those surges of threat, the memory of the machete swinging toward her would surface without warning, summoned by the adrenaline itself, as if her body had learned to connect fear directly to that single image. Each time she boards a bus, the cycle tightens: the trigger triggers her hypervigilance, and the hypervigilance triggers a fresh wave of the memory—the image of a machete swinging toward her—which in turn feeds her conviction that what happened to her was deeply unjust, that nothing was ever done, that the perpetrators still walk free. That sense of injustice makes her even more vigilant on the next bus ride.

Amara has come to believe that if she allows herself to think about the event in any detail, she will not be able to cope. That very belief made the memory more insistent: the more she told herself she could not handle it, the more the morning at the altar came back in full, brutal colour, as if to prove her right. So she avoids talking about it entirely. When fellow pastors ask about her journey, she changes the subject. When her husband tries to gently mention the names of people they lost, she leaves the room. She also avoids seeking medical or psychological help, because she fears a doctor would press her to describe what she saw, and she would then fall apart. Each thing she avoided — a question from a friend, a line in a book, a doctor’s waiting room — became a reminder in itself, a silent marker of what she could not face, so that the avoidance created new triggers out of the ordinary world around her. This avoidance, however, has a cost: the memories become more intrusively vivid when she is alone, and she finds herself reliving the sounds and the unreal quality of that morning. It also means her husband has grown weary of her silence; their conversations have become thin, and she knows he feels shut out.

What frightens Amara most is the feeling that she is no longer a person. She feels like an object—something that was acted upon, not a woman with a life and a calling. Once she saw herself that way, almost anything could trigger the sense of being acted upon again — a bus driver’s barked order, a stranger’s accidental shoulder, the sight of a man’s arm raised to signal a stop. This dehumanizing appraisal is triggered by the smallest things: a bus driver's abrupt stop, a man's raised voice, a kitchen knife lying on the counter. Each of these small triggers renews her belief that she is helpless and that her story is too terrible to speak. And the more she believes that, the more she watches for danger, the more she checks behind her, the more she wears her concealing clothing. The world has become a landscape of potential threats, and she is perpetually on guard. Feeling this unsafe all the time had quietly confirmed what she worked hardest to resist — that she was no longer a woman with a future, just someone waiting for the next terrible thing to happen.

After months of sleepless nights and a growing sense of isolation, Amara finally told her husband that she thinks she needs help. She is terrified of what a therapist might ask, but she is more afraid of losing the last connection she has left—the quiet man who shares her bed and who has been waiting for her to say something. She is not sure she can tell him what happened, but she knows she cannot go on like this.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals causally lead to the memory; instead, memory triggers negative appraisals or maladaptive strategies trigger memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals causally lead to triggers; triggers are described as triggering negative appraisals, not the reverse.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph conveys that threat directly triggers the memory; the memory is triggered by hypervigilance or triggers, not by threat itself.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that threat causally leads to negative appraisals; negative appraisals are triggered by memory or triggers, not by threat directly.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies causally lead to triggers; triggers lead to maladaptive strategies, and maladaptive strategies lead to threat, but not to new triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
